power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: To estimate the required sample size, a Monte Carlo power analysis was conducted based on the standardized path coefficients obtained from Study 1 (Muthén & Muthén, 2002) using the Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Indirect Effects web application (Schoemann et al., 2017). The simulation included 1,000 replications and 20,000 Monte Carlo draws per replication, with a target power of 0.80 and a 95% confidence level. Results indicated that the power to detect both indirect effects (via hopeful and anxious sentiments) reached target power at approximately N = 1,000, suggesting that a sample of around one thousand participants would be sufficient to reliably detect the mediation effects in this model.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: An exploratory study on selective exposure to environmental messages
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
People encounter a vast amount of information daily, but not all of it is received or processed. The behavior of preferentially engaging with specific information from the available options is known as selective exposure.
This study aims to investigate how selective exposure to environmental messages with varying valences influences individuals' emotional stances (e.g., hope, optimism, anxiety, worry) toward environmental issues. Additionally, it explores whether the self-relevance of the messages moderates this effect.
Please refer to the "Conditions” and “Dependent Variable” sections for a comprehensive understanding of the study design.
This study includes the following hypotheses:
H1: The effects of selective exposure to environmental messages on emotional stances to this issue is influenced by message valence. Specifically:
•	H1a: Exposure to positive environmental messages is expected to increase positive emotions toward this issue, such as hope and optimism.
•	H1b: Exposure to negative environmental messages is expected to increase negative emotions towards this issue, such as anxiety and worry.
H2: The effects of selective exposure to environmental messages on emotional stances to this issue (both positive and negative) will be moderated by the self-relevance of the message, with stronger effects observed for human-related messages compared to animal-related messages.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they will be measured.
1.	Selective Exposure
In our hypotheses, the indicators of selective exposure function as independent variables. However, we also explore several research questions where these indicators serve as dependent variables.
Selective exposure will be measured in the following way (Westerwick, Johnson, & Knobloch-Westerwick, 2017):
•	Message selection: For each article, whether participants chose to read it or not (binary).
•	Reading time: The duration (in seconds) spent reading each chosen article.
2.	Change in Emotional Stance 
Participants will report their emotional stances (hope, optimism, worry, anxiety) towards two societal issues (i.e., health and environment) both before and after the selective exposure task. For example, they will respond to items such as:
"When thinking about your own life situation in the next 20 years, to what extent do you feel [hopeful, optimistic, worried, anxious] regarding environmental issues?"
The increase in emotional stance will be calculated as the difference between the post-exposure and pre-exposure score.
table.study_design_overview:
In this study, participants are presented with a grid with 16 headlines of articles and are asked to choose those that they want to read. These articles with corresponding headlines serve as message materials. In addition to headlines/articles with environmental messages, participants can choose to read articles with health-related messages. Health messages serve as a distractor. The headlines/articles are structured using a 2 (valence: positive vs. negative content) × 2 (self-relevance: animal vs. human focus) × 2 (topic: health vs. environment) factorial design, resulting in eight conditions, each represented by a pair of headlines/articles. 
For example, in the condition with positive valence, animal focus, and environmental topic, the article headlines are:
• Older elephants in East Africa face threats from climate change
• Higher temperatures threaten sea turtle hatchling production
Participants will be exposed to all 16 headlines at once. All article headlines will be displayed on an overview page, allowing participants to choose which articles they want to read. When clicked a new window will open to present the associated article. There will be a set time window for the selective exposure task for 10minutes.
table.statistical_tests:
In this study, we adopt a fully exploratory data analysis approach to test our hypotheses and research questions (Ledgerwood, 2019). 
Following the exploratory analysis and deriving preliminary conclusions, we plan to conduct a second, confirmatory study. This confirmatory study will preregister both hypotheses and the analysis plan to ensure transparency, rigor and robustness in our research process.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Instructed response items are included as attention checks, with one placed before and one after the selective exposure task. Participants who fail one or more attention checks will be excluded from the analysis.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size is set at 250 participants.
table.name: An exploratory study on selective exposure to environmental messages
table.additional_comments:
Exploratory purposes 
1.	In our hypotheses, we predict how environmental message features, such as valence and self-relevance, might impact emotional stances. Additionally, we are interested in Exploratory Question 1: Do message features affect people's engagement preferences?
Specifically:
•	Do people prefer environmental messages or health messages?
•	… positive messages or negative messages?
•	… human-related messages or animal-related messages? 
2.	We also collect other variables that might explain preferences for environmental messages, such as baseline (pre-exposure) emotional stances (i.e., hope, optimism, anxiety, and worry), as well as other motivational factors such as interest, curiosity, urgency, and perceived knowledge regarding environmental issues.
Exploratory Question 2: Do emotional stances, interest, curiosity, urgency, and perceived knowledge regarding environmental issues influence people’s selective exposure to environmental messages?
For example, curiosity will be measured with the item: “When thinking about the current state of the world in terms of environmental issues, how curious do you feel?”
3.	We are interested in whether exposure to environmental messages influences the intention to seek further environmental information.
Exploratory Question 3: Does greater selective exposure to environmental messages leads to a stronger intention to seek information?
Information seeking intention will be measured by 5 items, such as: I plan to seek information about environmental issues in the near future” (Kahlor, 2010). 
4.	We aim to explore whether increases in emotional stances — both positive and negative — are associated with the intention to seek further environmental information. 
Exploratory Question 4: Do increases in hope, optimism, anxiety, or worry towards environmental issues relate to the intention to seek environmental information, serving as a mediator between selective exposure and information-seeking behavior?

Article questions
We designed multiple-choice questions with three options tailored to the content of each article to explore the extent to which participants read the articles. Based on participants’ reading selections, these questions will be presented randomly after the task, with up to three questions. This approach could serve as a possible attention check in follow-up studies to assess whether participants carefully read the articles they chose.

References
Kahlor, L. (2010). PRISM: a planned risk information seeking model. Health Commun, 25(4), 345-356. doi:10.1080/10410231003775172
Ledgerwood, A. (2019). New developments in research methods. Advanced social psychology. 
Westerwick, A., Johnson, B. K., & Knobloch-Westerwick, S. (2017). Change Your Ways: Fostering Health Attitudes Toward Change Through Selective Exposure to Online Health Messages. Health Commun, 32(5), 639-649. doi:10.1080/10410236.2016.1160319

table.title: A confirmatory study on selective exposure to environmental messages
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
In a preregistered exploratory study(https://osf.io/9c82y), we employed a selective exposure paradigm to gain preliminary insights into how engagement with environmental messages of varying valence influences individuals’ emotional stances toward environmental issues, their subsequent information-seeking behaviors, and the moderating role of self-relevance in these processes. In the present confirmatory study, we adopt the same research design to attempt to replicate the findings from the exploratory study, and to test the following hypotheses:

Hypothesis 1:
In the environmental domain, exposure to negative messages is effective in changing people’s emotional stances toward environmental issues, and this effect is moderated by perceived self-relevance. Specifically:
H1a: Exposure to more self-relevant negative messages (e.g., human-related) is expected to result in a greater decrease in positive emotional stances, compared to less self-relevant messages (e.g., animal-related).
H1b: Exposure to more self-relevant negative messages (e.g., human-related) is expected to result in a greater increase in negative emotional stances, compared to less self-relevant messages (e.g., animal-related).

Hypothesis 2:
Exposure to negative human-related messages simultaneously influences information-seeking intentions through two opposing pathways, with emotional stances serving as mediators. Specifically:
H2a: Exposure to negative human-related messages is expected to decrease positive emotional stances, which in turn reduce information seeking intentions.
H2b: Exposure to negative human-related messages is expected to increase negative emotional stances, which in turn promote information seeking intentions.

Hypothesis 3:
Individuals with greater self-reported knowledge about environmental issues are more likely to select positive human-related messages.
table.design_dependent_variables:
1.	Selective Exposure
In our hypotheses, the indicators of selective exposure function as independent variables. However, we also explore several research questions where these indicators serve as dependent variables.
Selective exposure will be measured in the following way (Westerwick, Johnson, & Knobloch-Westerwick, 2017):
•	Message selection: For each article, whether participants chose to read it or not (binary).
•	Reading time: The duration (in seconds) spent reading each chosen article.
2.	Emotional Stances 
Participants will report their emotional stances (positive: hope, optimism; negative: worry, anxiety) towards environment issues both before and after the selective exposure task. For example, they will respond to items such as:
"When thinking about your own life situation in the next 20 years, to what extent do you feel [hopeful, optimistic, worried, anxious] regarding environmental issues?"

3.	Perceived Knowledge
Participants will report their perceived knowledge about environmental issues, measured by a single item:
“How much do you currently know about environmental issues?”

4.	Information Seeking Intention
In exploratory study, participants’ intentions to seek further information were measured using five items, following Kahlor (2010). The scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = .98), suggesting not only high reliability but also potential item redundancy. To keep the survey brief, we retained only one representative item in current study:  
“I intend to find more information about environmental issues soon.”
This item showed the highest average inter-item correlation (r = .93), the highest signal-to-noise ratio and the lowest inter-item variance suggesting that it most accurately and consistently reflected the underlying construct (i.e., information-seeking intention). Responses will be measured on a 7-point Likert-type scale (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree).
table.study_design_overview:
In the selective exposure task, participants are presented with a grid of article headlines and asked to choose which articles they would like to read. In addition to articles containing environmental messages, participants may also select articles related to health topics, which serve as control content.
The headline-article pairs are structured using a 2 (valence: positive vs. negative content) × 2 (self-relevance: animal vs. human focus) × 2 (topic: health vs. environment) factorial design, resulting in eight experimental conditions. Each condition includes two headline-article pairs.
For example, in the condition with positive valence and animal focus on environmental topics, the article headlines are:
• Older elephants in East Africa face threats from climate change
• Higher temperatures threaten sea turtle hatchling production
Participants will be exposed to all 16 headlines (covering all eight conditions) simultaneously. All headlines will be displayed on an overview page, allowing participants to freely select which articles they wish to read. Upon clicking a headline, a new window will open displaying the full article. Participants will have a total of 10 minutes to complete the selective exposure task.
table.statistical_tests:
For Hypothesis 1:
Following the approach of Westerwick et al. (2017), within each message condition (i.e., negative human-related condition), we will calculate the number of articles each participant chose to read. These counts will be used as four separate predictors in the analyses, 
Controlling for baseline measures (i.e., pre-exposure positive and negative emotional stances) and other control variables (i.e., perceived knowledge, curiosity, interest, urgency), we will conduct separate regression analyses predicting post-exposure positive emotional stances and negative emotional stances. 
Based on our hypotheses, selecting more negative human-related articles is expected to predict lower post-exposure positive emotions and higher post-exposure negative emotions more strongly than selecting negative animal-related articles.

For Hypothesis 2:
We will test a parallel mediation model, with four message selection variables (the same as for H1) simultaneously entered as the independent variables (X₁ to X₄), post-exposure positive emotional stances and negative emotional stances as two mediators (M₁ and M₂), and information-seeking intention as the dependent variable (Y). Baseline measures and other control variables (the same as for H1) will be included as covariates in the regression analyses.
Based on our hypotheses, exposure to more negative human-related messages is expected to lower positive emotion stances and raise negative emotion stances, which will respectively decrease and increase the intention to seek further information.

For Hypothesis 3:
Perceived knowledge will serve as the independent variable (IV), and positive human-related message selections will serve as the dependent variable (DV). Controlling baseline measures and other control variables (the same as for H1 and H2 except perceived knowledge), we will conduct Poisson regression analyses. A backward elimination method will be applied to reduce multicollinearity and to identify the most influential predictors. 
Based on our hypotheses, participants who perceive themselves as more knowledgeable are expected to select mores positive human-related messages during the task.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Instructed response items are included as attention checks, with one placed before and one after the selective exposure task. Participants who fail one or more attention checks will be excluded from the analysis.
Furthermore, participants who do not engage sufficiently with the selective exposure task (i.e., who select fewer than four articles to read) will also be excluded.
table.sample_size:
Detecting indirect effects generally requires larger sample sizes. Thus, based on the parallel mediation results from the exploratory study, we conducted a Monte Carlo power analysis specifically targeting the indirect effects. The simulation was conducted with 10,000 replications and 10,000 draws per replication, using the parameter estimates for the indirect effect paths obtained from the exploratory study. Assuming an alpha level of .05 and aiming for a statistical power of .80, the results indicated that a minimum of 950 participants is required to reliably detect the indirect effects.
Accordingly, we will recruit a sample of 1,000 participants in the confirmatory study to allow for potential exclusions.
table.name: A confirmatory study on selective exposure to environmental messages
table.additional_comments:
1.	In the exploratory study, the two selective exposure indicators — message selection and reading time — showed similar patterns of results. Therefore, in the confirmatory study, we will focus on message selection as the primary indicator. Findings related to reading time will be examined for exploratory purposes and reported as supplementary results.
2.	We also collect the same set of data for health-related issues to examine whether the hypothesized relationships hold within the health domain.
3.	Beyond the findings specifically related to negative human-related messages, we also explore the effects of other message types—namely, positive human-related messages, negative animal-related messages and positive animal-related messages. Specifically, we will explore whether 1) these messages influence participants’ emotional stances toward environmental issues (i.e., similar to the effect proposed in H1); 2) this process subsequently influences participants’ intentions to seek further environmental information (i.e., as proposed in H2); and 3) perceived knowledge, baseline emotional stances or other factors (curiosity, interest, and urgency) predict participants’ selection of these messages.
4.	Building on the procedure used in the exploratory study, we collected participants’ levels of curiosity, interest, and urgency toward environmental issues prior to the selective exposure task as control variables. In the confirmatory study, these variables will also be measured after the task to explore potential changes. This allows us to explore, for example, whether exposure to negative human-related messages may increase participants' curiosity, interest, or urgency regarding environmental issues.
5.	Finally, four open-ended questions will be included to investigate participants' motivations for engaging with, or avoiding, positive and negative environmental content (e.g., news articles, documentaries, expositions, books).

Analyses related to purposes 4 will be conducted using an exploratory data analysis approach (Ledgerwood, 2019). The data collected with the open-ended questions will be analyzed using a qualitative strategy.

table.title: An exploratory study on selective exposure to environmental messages
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
People encounter a vast amount of information daily, but not all of it is received or processed. The behavior of preferentially engaging with specific information from the available options is known as selective exposure.
This study aims to investigate how selective exposure to environmental messages with varying valences influences individuals' emotional stances (e.g., hope, optimism, anxiety, worry) toward environmental issues. Additionally, it explores whether the self-relevance of the messages moderates this effect.
Please refer to the "Conditions” and “Dependent Variable” sections for a comprehensive understanding of the study design.
This study includes the following hypotheses:
H1: The effects of selective exposure to environmental messages on emotional stances to this issue is influenced by message valence. Specifically:
•	H1a: Exposure to positive environmental messages is expected to increase positive emotions toward this issue, such as hope and optimism.
•	H1b: Exposure to negative environmental messages is expected to increase negative emotions towards this issue, such as anxiety and worry.
H2: The effects of selective exposure to environmental messages on emotional stances to this issue (both positive and negative) will be moderated by the self-relevance of the message, with stronger effects observed for human-related messages compared to animal-related messages.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they will be measured.
1.	Selective Exposure
In our hypotheses, the indicators of selective exposure function as independent variables. However, we also explore several research questions where these indicators serve as dependent variables.
Selective exposure will be measured in the following way (Westerwick, Johnson, & Knobloch-Westerwick, 2017):
•	Message selection: For each article, whether participants chose to read it or not (binary).
•	Reading time: The duration (in seconds) spent reading each chosen article.
2.	Change in Emotional Stance 
Participants will report their emotional stances (hope, optimism, worry, anxiety) towards two societal issues (i.e., health and environment) both before and after the selective exposure task. For example, they will respond to items such as:
"When thinking about your own life situation in the next 20 years, to what extent do you feel [hopeful, optimistic, worried, anxious] regarding environmental issues?"
The increase in emotional stance will be calculated as the difference between the post-exposure and pre-exposure score.
table.study_design_overview:
In this study, participants are presented with a grid with 16 headlines of articles and are asked to choose those that they want to read. These articles with corresponding headlines serve as message materials. In addition to headlines/articles with environmental messages, participants can choose to read articles with health-related messages. Health messages serve as a distractor. The headlines/articles are structured using a 2 (valence: positive vs. negative content) × 2 (self-relevance: animal vs. human focus) × 2 (topic: health vs. environment) factorial design, resulting in eight conditions, each represented by a pair of headlines/articles. 
For example, in the condition with positive valence, animal focus, and environmental topic, the article headlines are:
• Older elephants in East Africa face threats from climate change
• Higher temperatures threaten sea turtle hatchling production
Participants will be exposed to all 16 headlines at once. All article headlines will be displayed on an overview page, allowing participants to choose which articles they want to read. When clicked a new window will open to present the associated article. There will be a set time window for the selective exposure task for 10minutes.
table.statistical_tests:
In this study, we adopt a fully exploratory data analysis approach to test our hypotheses and research questions (Ledgerwood, 2019). 
Following the exploratory analysis and deriving preliminary conclusions, we plan to conduct a second, confirmatory study. This confirmatory study will preregister both hypotheses and the analysis plan to ensure transparency, rigor and robustness in our research process.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Instructed response items are included as attention checks, with one placed before and one after the selective exposure task. Participants who fail one or more attention checks will be excluded from the analysis.
table.sample_size: Our target sample size is set at 250 participants.
table.name: An exploratory study on selective exposure to environmental messages
table.additional_comments:
Exploratory purposes 
1.	In our hypotheses, we predict how environmental message features, such as valence and self-relevance, might impact emotional stances. Additionally, we are interested in Exploratory Question 1: Do message features affect people's engagement preferences?
Specifically:
•	Do people prefer environmental messages or health messages?
•	… positive messages or negative messages?
•	… human-related messages or animal-related messages? 
2.	We also collect other variables that might explain preferences for environmental messages, such as baseline (pre-exposure) emotional stances (i.e., hope, optimism, anxiety, and worry), as well as other motivational factors such as interest, curiosity, urgency, and perceived knowledge regarding environmental issues.
Exploratory Question 2: Do emotional stances, interest, curiosity, urgency, and perceived knowledge regarding environmental issues influence people’s selective exposure to environmental messages?
For example, curiosity will be measured with the item: “When thinking about the current state of the world in terms of environmental issues, how curious do you feel?”
3.	We are interested in whether exposure to environmental messages influences the intention to seek further environmental information.
Exploratory Question 3: Does greater selective exposure to environmental messages leads to a stronger intention to seek information?
Information seeking intention will be measured by 5 items, such as: I plan to seek information about environmental issues in the near future” (Kahlor, 2010). 
4.	We aim to explore whether increases in emotional stances — both positive and negative — are associated with the intention to seek further environmental information. 
Exploratory Question 4: Do increases in hope, optimism, anxiety, or worry towards environmental issues relate to the intention to seek environmental information, serving as a mediator between selective exposure and information-seeking behavior?

Article questions
We designed multiple-choice questions with three options tailored to the content of each article to explore the extent to which participants read the articles. Based on participants’ reading selections, these questions will be presented randomly after the task, with up to three questions. This approach could serve as a possible attention check in follow-up studies to assess whether participants carefully read the articles they chose.

References
Kahlor, L. (2010). PRISM: a planned risk information seeking model. Health Commun, 25(4), 345-356. doi:10.1080/10410231003775172
Ledgerwood, A. (2019). New developments in research methods. Advanced social psychology. 
Westerwick, A., Johnson, B. K., & Knobloch-Westerwick, S. (2017). Change Your Ways: Fostering Health Attitudes Toward Change Through Selective Exposure to Online Health Messages. Health Commun, 32(5), 639-649. doi:10.1080/10410236.2016.1160319

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").


stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 160 columns across 2 data files.
#### Careless Responding

171 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **171 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 3 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  2 of 3 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  10 installable dependencies detected.
- 3709 statistics stored from the extracted output; 55 of 75 reported tests matched (73.3%).

ethics_statements: Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethical Review Board of the University of Amsterdam, and all participants provided informed consent prior to participation.
Ethical approval for this research was granted by the Ethical Review Board of the University of Amsterdam, and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation
live_data_statements: However, much of this work typically relies on experimental designs in which participants are passively exposed to predefined message types selected by researchers, rather than being allowed to choose among messages, momentary feelings of anxiety may become incorporated into a broader climate-related anxious sentiment (Maran & Begotti, 2021; Shao & Yu, 2023).
A total of 291 participants were recruited from the United Kingdom through the Prolific platform.

Eight participants were excluded for failing the attention check or for not completing the task as instructed, resulting in a final sample of 283 participants (163 women, 113 men, 2 non-binary/third gender, 5 preferred not to say).
Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethical Review Board of the University of Amsterdam, and all participants provided informed consent prior to participation.
For example, for hopeful sentiment, participants were asked: When thinking about your own life situation in the next 20 years, to what extent do you feel hopeful regarding environmental issues?
After the baseline measurements, participants completed a selective exposure task adapted from Westerwick et al. (2017).
On an initial overview page, participants were presented with article headlines displayed as clickable rectangular buttons in a randomized grid layout.
Participants were informed that they had 10 minutes to browse the articles and were encouraged to read those they found most interesting.
To ensure sufficient data quality, participants were required to read at least four articles.
After the selective exposure task, participants completed a short memory test on the articles they had read.
Finally, participants provided demographic information, including age, gender, and education levels.
To select suitable experimental stimuli, we conducted a two-stage pilot study with UK-based participants recruited through Prolific.

Given that each participant provided multiple count-based responses (0/1/2) across experimental conditions, we employed Poisson mixed-effects models with random intercepts for participants to analyze participants' selection behavior across various message types.
A total of 1,034 participants were recruited from the United Kingdom via the Prolific platform.
Ethical approval for this research was granted by the Ethical Review Board of the University of Amsterdam, and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation
Next, participants completed the selective exposure task.
Forty-four participants (4.4%) selected no environmental articles.

````
> library(lavaan)
> library(ggplot2)
> monte_carlo_power_curve <- function(Ns, sims = 1000, alpha = 0.05) {
>   
>   # Effect sizes based on assumed standardized path coefficients
>   a1 <- -0.15
>   b1 <- 0.21
>   a2 <- 0.09
>   b2 <- 0.37
>   c_prime <- 0.01
>   
>   # Lavaan parallel mediation model
>   model <- '
>     M1 ~ a1*X
>     M2 ~ a2*X
>     Y ~ b1*M1 + b2*M2 + c*X
> 
>     ind1 := a1*b1
>     ind2 := a2*b2
>   '
>   
>   results <- list()
>   
>   for (n in Ns) {
>     
>     sig_ind1 <- 0
>     sig_ind2 <- 0
>     
>     for (i in 1:sims) {
>       
>       # Simulate data
>       X <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)
>       M1 <- a1 * X + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
>       M2 <- a2 * X + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
>       Y <- b1 * M1 + b2 * M2 + c_prime * X + rnorm(n, 0, 1)
>       
>       dat <- data.frame(X, M1, M2, Y)
>       
>       # Fit mediation model
>       fit <- tryCatch({
>         lavaan::sem(model, data = dat, fixed.x = FALSE)
>       }, error = function(e) NULL)
>       
>       if (!is.null(fit)) {
>         pe <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit)
>         
>         p_ind1 <- pe$pvalue[pe$label == "ind1"]
>         p_ind2 <- pe$pvalue[pe$label == "ind2"]
>         
>         if (length(p_ind1) == 1 && p_ind1 < alpha) sig_ind1 <- sig_ind1 + 1
>         if (length(p_ind2) == 1 && p_ind2 < alpha) sig_ind2 <- sig_ind2 + 1
>       }
>     }
>     
>     results[[as.character(n)]] <- data.frame(
>       N = n,
>       power_ind1 = sig_ind1 / sims,
>       power_ind2 = sig_ind2 / sims
>     )
>   }
>   
>   return(do.call(rbind, results))
> }
````

text.text: Environmental problems are intensifying, prompting expanded public communication efforts to raise awareness and motivate pro-environmental behavior.
However, meaningful engagement with environmental messages is often selective, as people actively choose among many competing messages.
In this paper, we examined how active engagement with environmental messages related to affective orientations (i.e., sentiments) towards environmental issues.
Through a selective exposure paradigm, participants selected from four types of environmental messages varying in valence (positive vs. negative) and personal relevance (human vs. animal).
We expected that engagement with these messages would be associated with changes in hopeful and anxious sentiments toward environmental issues.
These sentiment shifts, in turn, were expected to predict the likelihood of participants seeking further environmental information.
In an initial exploratory study (N = 283), participants' selection of the different kinds of environmental messages showed no direct effect on environmental information-seeking intentions.
Further analyses revealed two competing indirect paths: (a) increased seeking intentions via enhanced anxious sentiments and (b) reduced seeking intentions via diminished hopeful sentiments.
These patterns were replicated in a confirmatory study (N = 1,009), demonstrating their robustness.
Together, these findings suggest that the effectiveness of environmental communication is not limited to valencecongruent sentiments.
Instead, the balance of emotional reactions that messages trigger shapes information-seeking behavior.

Environmental problems, including extreme weather, biodiversity loss, and ocean pollution, are getting worse (UNEP, 2025), threatening both ecosystems and human well-being (Nesmith et al., 2021; Yang, 2025).
text.formatted: Environmental problems, including extreme weather, biodiversity loss, and ocean pollution, are getting worse (UNEP, 2025), threatening both ecosystems and human well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Nesmith et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Yang, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Environmental communication plays a crucial role in sustaining public attention to climate and ecological crises (Ter Mors et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Environmental communication plays a crucial role in sustaining public attention to climate and ecological crises <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Ter Mors et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: However, greater access to information doesn't always translate into more action addressing a societal problem (Ejaz et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, greater access to information doesn't always translate into more action addressing a societal problem <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Ejaz et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A growing number of studies are exploring which message features are most effective in attracting attention and encouraging engagement with environmental issues, with the ultimate goal of creating better environmental communication strategies to drive behavior change.
Building on this work, the present research uses a selective exposure paradigm to investigate people's active choices among different environmental messages.

Across two studies, participants chose among positive and negative environmental messages that focused on consequences for either humans or animals, with human-focused messages designed to be more personally relevant.

To examine the implications of these choices, we assessed changes in participants' broader affective evaluations of environmental issues, which we conceptualize as sentiments, as well as their subsequent informationseeking intentions.
We expected participants' message choices to be associated with changes in hopeful and anxious sentiments.
We also tested whether these sentiments predicted subsequent intentions to seek further environmental information.
Without exposure, media messages cannot produce any effects on audiences (McGuire, 1985).
text.formatted: Without exposure, media messages cannot produce any effects on audiences <ref type="bibr">(McGuire, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, examining the effects of messages requires consideration of whether and how individuals engage with the content available to them.

Prior research has shown that message features such as valence and personal relevance shape audience responses, including risk perception and pro-environmental intentions (Jacobson et al., 2019; Rosenthal & Ai, 2024; Scannell & Gifford, 2013; Troy et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Prior research has shown that message features such as valence and personal relevance shape audience responses, including risk perception and pro-environmental intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Jacobson et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Rosenthal & Ai, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Scannell & Gifford, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Troy et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, much of this work typically relies on experimental designs in which participants are passively exposed to predefined message types selected by researchers, rather than being allowed to choose among messages, momentary feelings of anxiety may become incorporated into a broader climate-related anxious sentiment (Maran & Begotti, 2021; Shao & Yu, 2023).
text.formatted: However, much of this work typically relies on experimental designs in which participants are passively exposed to predefined message types selected by researchers, rather than being allowed to choose among messages, momentary feelings of anxiety may become incorporated into a broader climate-related anxious sentiment <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Maran & Begotti, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Shao & Yu, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, repeated exposure to hope appeals in environmental communications may evoke momentary hopeful responses, which can gradually consolidate into more stable hopeful sentiment that encourages engagement with environmental problems (Chadwick, 2015).
text.formatted: Likewise, repeated exposure to hope appeals in environmental communications may evoke momentary hopeful responses, which can gradually consolidate into more stable hopeful sentiment that encourages engagement with environmental problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chadwick, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, individuals may come to hold relatively stable sentiments toward environmental issues.
These sentiments may influence not only how environmental issues are perceived, but also individuals' openness to further information engagement (Kahlor, 2010).
text.formatted: These sentiments may influence not only how environmental issues are perceived, but also individuals' openness to further information engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kahlor, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This makes sentiment a particularly useful lens for understanding the broader affective implications of selective engagement with environmental messages.
To examine how people's message choices may relate to environmental sentiments, we focus on two key attributes of environmental messages: valence and personal relevance.
Message valence carries the "emotional charge" of environmental news, labeling it as either a warning of damage or a sign of (potential) success.
Negative valence centers on the breakdown of ecosystems, threats, and harm, whereas positive valence highlights recovery and effective environmental action.
Environmental communication is often dominated by negative messages, which can heighten risk perception and awareness (Diamond & Urbanski, 2022; Troy et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Environmental communication is often dominated by negative messages, which can heighten risk perception and awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Diamond & Urbanski, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Troy et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, when such messages emphasize adverse impacts without offering actionable solutions, they may elicit defensive responses or information avoidance (Brosch, 2021; Ettinger et al., 2021).
text.formatted: However, when such messages emphasize adverse impacts without offering actionable solutions, they may elicit defensive responses or information avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brosch, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Ettinger et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Scholars have therefore advocated for more positive, solution-oriented approaches, such as hope-based communication, which highlight efficacy and actionable pathways (Chadwick, 2015; Troy et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Scholars have therefore advocated for more positive, solution-oriented approaches, such as hope-based communication, which highlight efficacy and actionable pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Chadwick, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Troy et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence suggests that these approaches can increase interest in climate protection and pro-environmental intentions (Baden et al., 2019; Chadwick, 2015).
text.formatted: Evidence suggests that these approaches can increase interest in climate protection and pro-environmental intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baden et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Chadwick, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these studies suggest that message valence is related to how audiences perceive and respond to environmental information.

A second important message attribute is personal relevance, which refers to the extent to which information connects to individuals' self-concept, goals, values, or lived experiences (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986; Schäfer et al., 2020).
text.formatted: A second important message attribute is personal relevance, which refers to the extent to which information connects to individuals' self-concept, goals, values, or lived experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Petty & Cacioppo, 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Schäfer et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In general, information perceived as more personally relevant tends to attract more attention and deeper processing (Arlt et al., 2018; El Hedhli & Zourrig, 2023; Liu & Yang, 2023).
text.formatted: In general, information perceived as more personally relevant tends to attract more attention and deeper processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arlt et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">El Hedhli & Zourrig, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Liu & Yang, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In the environmental domain, climate change is more likely to attract attention and engagement when it is perceived as a personal rather than merely societal threat (Ma et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In the environmental domain, climate change is more likely to attract attention and engagement when it is perceived as a personal rather than merely societal threat <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Ma et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, environmental issues that are experienced as geographically close rather than distant tend to elicit higher risk perceptions and more intense emotional responses (Mărgărint et al., 2021; Milfont et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Similarly, environmental issues that are experienced as geographically close rather than distant tend to elicit higher risk perceptions and more intense emotional responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Mărgărint et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Milfont et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Sun et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, findings on message valence and personal relevance suggest that both may be related to engagement with environmental information and how it is perceived and experienced.
We reasoned that, in a selective exposure context, the valence and personal relevance of the messages people select may therefore be related to their subsequent environmental sentiments.

The primary aim of the current study was to examine how selective engagement with environmental messages relates to changes in sentiments toward environmental issues, as well as whether these sentiments would predict information-seeking intentions.

We expected that the relationship between participants' selective exposure to environmental messages and their sentiments, that is, their affective orientation towards environmental issues, would vary by message valence (H1).

Specifically, selective exposure to positive environmental messages was expected to be associated with increases in hopeful and optimistic sentiments (H1a), whereas selective exposure to negative environmental messages was expected to be associated with increases in anxious and worried sentiments (H1b).
Furthermore, affective responses toward societal issues depend on how people view an event's relevance to their own concerns and goals (Brosch, 2021; Moors et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Furthermore, affective responses toward societal issues depend on how people view an event's relevance to their own concerns and goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brosch, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Moors et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, sentiments toward environmental issues elicited by climate-related messages may depend on the extent to which individuals see such messages as personally relevant.

Building on this perspective, we hypothesized that the relationship between selective exposure to environmental messages and sentiments (hopeful, optimistic, anxious, and worried) toward environmental issues would be moderated by the personal relevance of the message, with stronger associations for highly relevant messages than for less personally relevant messages (H2).

Finally, beyond sentiments, we were interested in the behavioral implications of exposure to environmental messages, particularly in terms of individuals' intentions to seek further environmental information.
This could form a dynamic feedback loop in which initial message exposure is linked to information seeking, which may in turn be associated with further exposure to environmental messages.

Based on prior theories and empirical research on information seeking, affective responses such as feelings of threat, worry and hope, play a central role in motivating information-seeking intentions (Kahlor, 2010; Yang & Kahlor, 2012), including in environmental contexts (Choo, 2023; Kahlor et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Based on prior theories and empirical research on information seeking, affective responses such as feelings of threat, worry and hope, play a central role in motivating information-seeking intentions <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kahlor, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Yang & Kahlor, 2012)</ref>, including in environmental contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Choo, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Kahlor et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: As broader, issue-specific affective orientations, sentiments may similarly serve as predictors of information-seeking intentions.
However, existing literature offers less clear guidance on whether sentiments are likely to motivate further information seeking, and if so, in what direction.

Accordingly, we posed the following research question: How are post-exposure sentiments, both hopeful and anxious, associated with individuals' intentions to seek further environmental information (RQ)?
In this paper, we adopted a stepwise exploratory-confirmatory approach to address our hypotheses and research question.
The exploratory study was conducted to provide an initial test of the hypothesized model and to identify potential relationships among key variables.
The results were then used to inform power calculations and sample size estimation for a subsequent confirmatory study (Button et al., 2013).

text.text: Results for additional exploratory questions preregistered on OSF are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
A total of 291 participants were recruited from the United Kingdom through the Prolific platform.

Eight participants were excluded for failing the attention check or for not completing the task as instructed, resulting in a final sample of 283 participants (163 women, 113 men, 2 non-binary/third gender, 5 preferred not to say).
Participants ranged in age from 18 to 83 years (M = 37.42, SD = 12.52).
Most participants held at least a bachelor's degree (38.9% bachelor's, 23.3% graduate or professional).
As Study 1 was exploratory, the sample size was guided by previous research on selective exposure rather than by an a-priori power analysis (Luong et al., 2021).
text.formatted: As Study 1 was exploratory, the sample size was guided by previous research on selective exposure rather than by an a-priori power analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Luong et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Participants received 2.70 UK pounds for completing the study, which took approximately 18 minutes.
Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethical Review Board of the University of Amsterdam, and all participants provided informed consent prior to participation.
A content warning was included to specify that some of the articles included negative content.
The overall procedure is illustrated in Figure 2A.
text.formatted: The overall procedure is illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure">2A</ref>.

text.text: Sentiments.
Before the selective exposure task, participants reported their baseline sentiments toward environmental issues.
Sentiment was conceptualized as an affective orientation that integrates discrete emotional experiences with a relatively enduring evaluative attitude towards a specific issue.
The present study operationalized this construct through four emotions felt towards environmental issues in the context of their future consequences.

Worry and anxiety captured persistent concern about environmental risks (Bechtoldt & Schermelleh-Engel, 2025; Maran & Begotti, 2021; Verplanken et al., 2020), whereas hope and optimism reflected sustained expectations for environmental improvement (Lee et al., 2017; McAfee et al., 2019; Zeier et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Worry and anxiety captured persistent concern about environmental risks <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bechtoldt & Schermelleh-Engel, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Maran & Begotti, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Verplanken et al., 2020)</ref>, whereas hope and optimism reflected sustained expectations for environmental improvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Lee et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">McAfee et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Zeier et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These emotions were selected to represent distinct yet complementary sentiments toward environmental issues.
Each sentiment was assessed using a single-item, 100-point scale ranging from 1 (not at all) and 100 (extremely).
For example, for hopeful sentiment, participants were asked: When thinking about your own life situation in the next 20 years, to what extent do you feel hopeful regarding environmental issues?
Because environmental issues often involve long-term risks and prospects for improvement, the 20-year framing anchored participants' current feelings within this longer-term horizon.
The items therefore assessed participants' current sentiments toward environmental issues in the context of their longer-term personal future, rather than how they expected to feel in the future.
To minimize potential order effects, the presentation order of the four sentiments was counterbalanced across participants following a Latinsquare design.
We measured several control variables, namely curiosity, interest, urgency, and perceived knowledge regarding environmental issues.
These variables were included to account for individual differences in baseline engagement and motivation.
All items were assessed on 100-point scales ranging from 0 (not at all) to 100 (extremely).
Item wordings are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
After the baseline measurements, participants completed a selective exposure task adapted from Westerwick et al. (2017).
text.formatted: After the baseline measurements, participants completed a selective exposure task adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Westerwick et al. (2017)</ref>.

text.text: On an initial overview page, participants were presented with article headlines displayed as clickable rectangular buttons in a randomized grid layout.
Participants were informed that they had 10 minutes to browse the articles and were encouraged to read those they found most interesting.
To ensure sufficient data quality, participants were required to read at least four articles.
Clicking a headline opened a pop-up window with the full article text, formatted in a newspaper-style layout.
After reading the article, participants closed the pop-up window and returned to the overview page to select another article.
The headline selection and article reading screens are shown in Figure 2B.
text.formatted: The headline selection and article reading screens are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>.

text.text: During the task, participants could read new articles, revisit previously read articles, or, when a minimum of four articles were chosen, decide not to read further.
Participants' article selections were tracked in real time using JavaScript-based monitoring.
Following Wojcieszak (2021), we measured exposure as the number of articles selected within each messages type.
The task automatically terminated after 10 minutes, redirecting participants to the next section of the study.
Two instructed response items were included as attention checks, with one placed before and one after the selective exposure task.
For instance, one item said To ensure you are paying attention, please select option C below.
Participants who failed one or more attention checks were excluded from the analysis.
Memory Test.
After the selective exposure task, participants completed a short memory test on the articles they had read.
The test consisted of three multiple-choice questions, each with three response options, based on a randomly drawn subset of the articles chosen by each participant.
This measure served as an indicator of participants' engagement with the content.
Participants then reported their sentiments toward environmental issues again, using the same items and response format as the baseline measurement.

Then, participants reported their intentions to seek further information about environmental topics, assessed using a five-item measure adapted from Kahlor (2010) (e.g., "I intend to find more information about environmental issues soon").
text.formatted: Then, participants reported their intentions to seek further information about environmental topics, assessed using a five-item measure adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kahlor (2010)</ref> (e.g., "I intend to find more information about environmental issues soon").

text.text: Responses were recorded on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).
Finally, participants provided demographic information, including age, gender, and education levels.

text.text: To select suitable experimental stimuli, we conducted a two-stage pilot study with UK-based participants recruited through Prolific.
We manipulated the personal relevance of messages by contrasting human-and animal-focused messages.

This approach builds on the fact that environmental degradation affects both human and animal welfare (Shivanna, 2022), allowing us to identify suitable stimulus material from real-world news sources.
text.formatted: This approach builds on the fact that environmental degradation affects both human and animal welfare <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Shivanna, 2022)</ref>, allowing us to identify suitable stimulus material from real-world news sources.

text.text: Health-related articles were included alongside the environmental articles as a control condition.

The materials were thus designed to vary systematically across three manipulated dimensions: Valence (positive vs. negative), Relevance (human vs. animal), and Topic (environment vs. health), while being match in terms of levels of interest, comprehensibility, and headline-article consistency.
Online news reports were selected from English-language outlets such as Euronews and Science Daily to provide a realistic context for participants' selective exposure decisions.
All texts were carefully edited to be 160-190 words long, ensuring that each could be read in under one minute given an average reading speed of ~200 words per minute (Rayner et al., 2016).
text.formatted: All texts were carefully edited to be 160-190 words long, ensuring that each could be read in under one minute given an average reading speed of ~200 words per minute <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Rayner et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Each article was paired with a headline, which was either adapted from the original source or newly generated to match the intended valence and personal relevance of the message.

Because the participants in the main study would choose which articles to read based on the headlines, the pilot study measured the attributes they expected the articles to have based on the headline, in terms of positivity, negativity, human focus, animal focus, environmental focus, and health focus.
These ratings also served to assess whether the intended manipulations were clearly conveyed by the headlines themselves.
For example, for each headline, participants rated how positive they expected an article associated with this headline to be.

The extent to which the articles reflected the attributes implied by the headlines was assessed through participants' post-reading ratings of headline-article consistency, based on two items: "How adequately does the article match the headline?"
and "How well does the headline summarize the article?"
Higher consistency ratings indicated greater alignment between the headline and article content.

Because the results the human-related materials did not perform satisfactorily in Stage 1, we selected and tested a revised set of candidate materials in Stage 2.
Based on the pilot study, we selected 16 articles: two for each combination of valence, relevance and topic type.
The selected articles were comparable in length (M = 178.31 words, SD = 7.92; range = 165-189 words), and the headlines were also similar in length (M = 7.81 words, SD = 1.56; range = 6-10 words).

For example, environmental articles included humanfocused positive stories such as Clean Energy Tech Slows Global Carbon Emissions Growth and animalfocused negative stories such as Older Elephants in East Africa Face Threats from Climate Change.

To verify that the human-animal manipulation effectively influenced perceived personal relevance, participants rated each headline on the item "To what extent do you expect that the article with this headline will be personally relevant to you?"
on a 0-100 scale.

Because each condition included two articles, a linear mixed-effects model was fitted to account for potential material-specific influences, with random intercepts for participants and articles and fixed effects for Relevance (human vs. animal) and Valence (positive vs. negative).

The analysis revealed a significant main effect of Relevance, β = 32.81, SE = 4.92, t(22.74) = 6.66, p < .001, indicating that participants rated human-related articles as significantly more personally relevant than animal-related ones.
text.formatted: The analysis revealed a significant main effect of Relevance, β = 32.81, SE = 4.92, t(22.74) = 6.66, p < .001, indicating that participants rated human-related articles as significantly more personally relevant than animal-related ones.

text.text: This effect was qualified by a significant Relevance × Valence interaction (β = -20.03, SE = 4.31, t(3.96) = -4.64, p = .010), which suggested that the difference in perceived personal relevance between human-and animal-related messages was smaller for positive articles.

Simple-effects analyses confirmed that human-related articles were rated significantly higher in personal relevance than animal-related ones, both in the negative condition (t(22.9) = 6.66, p < .001) and the positive condition (t(22.9) = 2.60, p = .016), confirming that the human-animal manipulation successfully affected perceived personal relevance.

We therefore aggregated them into composite scores of hopeful sentiment (hope and optimism) and anxious sentiment (anxiety and worry).
Similarly, since interest and curiosity were highly correlated (r = 0.96, p < .001), they were combined into a single composite score of interest.

text.text: We adapted the analytic strategy described by Westerwick et al. (2017).

text.text: Participants' selections of the four environmental message types (positive-human, negative-human, positive-animal, and negativeanimal) were entered simultaneously as predictors in two separate regression analyses, with post-exposure hopeful environmental sentiment and anxious environmental sentiment serving as the dependent variables, respectively.
Baseline measures of pre-exposure environmental sentiments, as well as interest, urgency, and perceived knowledge about environmental issues, were included as control variables.
This approach allowed Hypotheses 1 and 2 to be examined within the same models.

H1a was assessed by examining whether selections of positive-human and positive-animal messages were associated with higher post-exposure hopeful sentiment, whereas H1b was assessed by examining whether selections of negative-human and negative-animal messages were associated with higher postexposure anxious sentiment.

To test whether these associations differed by personal relevance (H2), we conducted linear hypothesis tests comparing the regression coefficients for human-and animal-related message selections, separately within the positive and negative message conditions and within each sentiment model.
These tests evaluated whether the two corresponding regression coefficients differed significantly and yielded the reported F statistics.
Thus, personal relevance was examined through coefficient comparisons rather than by including a conventional product-term interaction.
This strategy allowed participants' mixed selection patterns to be represented within a single participant-level model.
It also enabled the association of each message category with post-exposure sentiment to be estimated while accounting for selections from the other categories.
Next, we addressed the research question concerning how post-exposure sentiments would predict participants' subsequent environmental information-seeking intentions.

As post-exposure sentiments were expected to be associated with the types of messages participants chose to engage with, we specified a structural equation model with parallel indirect pathways to comprehensively map these relationships.

In this model, paths were specified from environmental message selection to post-exposure hopeful and anxious environmental sentiments, and from these sentiments to environmental informationseeking intentions, while controlling for baseline sentiments and other covariates.

All four message types (positive-human, negative-human, positive-animal, and negative-animal) were entered simultaneously as predictors to estimate their unique associations while accounting for shared variance across message categories.
Direct paths from message selection to information-seeking intentions were included for model completeness and were consistent with the preregistered exploratory objective.
The model was conducted in R (R Core Team, 2023) using the lavaan package (Rosseel, 2012).
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="2.2." >Results</head>

text.text: Memory performance was examined as a descriptive indicator of participants' processing of the selected articles.
Of the participants, 51.24% answered all three memory questions correctly, 34.28% answered two correctly, 13.07% answered one correctly, and 1.41% answered none correctly.
These descriptives suggest that most participants retained at least some information from the article content.

Participants with lower memory performance were retained in the main analyses because the selective exposure design was intended to approximate naturalistic information engagement, where variation in attention and message processing is expected.

As a sensitivity analysis, we excluded participants who answered none of the memory questions correctly; this yielded substantively unchanged results, and we therefore report the full-sample analyses.

On average, participants selected 7.40 (SD = 3.42) out of 16 available articles overall, including 3.50 (SD = 2.18) out of eight environmental messages, demonstrating that the browsing task allowed for selectivity in reading.

Given that each participant provided multiple count-based responses (0/1/2) across experimental conditions, we employed Poisson mixed-effects models with random intercepts for participants to analyze participants' selection behavior across various message types.

The results revealed a significant valence × personal relevance interaction, b = -0.44, SE = 0.13, z = -3.45, p < .001, indicating that participants' preference for positive versus negative messages differed between human-related and animal-related messages.
text.formatted: The results revealed a significant valence × personal relevance interaction, b = -0.44, SE = 0.13, z = -3.45, p < .001, indicating that participants' preference for positive versus negative messages differed between human-related and animal-related messages.

text.text: We conducted Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means.
Under negative valence, participants' selections did not differ between human-related (M = 0.86, SD = 0.83) and animal-related messages (M = 0.70, SD = 0.76), z = -2.10, p = .072.
Conversely, under positive valence, participants selected more animal-related (M = 1.08, SD = 0.78) than humanrelated messages (M = 0.85, SD = 0.78), z = 2.83, p = .009.
Participants' environmental message selections were generally mixed across both message dimensions.
Most chose both positive and negative articles (n = 193, 68.2%), but 63 people (22.3%) chose only positive articles and 17 (6.0%) chose only negative articles.

In terms of personal relevance, 180 participants (63.6%) selected both human-and animal-related articles, while 38 participants (13.4%) selected only human-related articles and 55 (19.4%) selected only animal-related articles.
Considering the two dimensions together, 153 participants (54.1%) made selections that included both valences and both personal-relevance categories.
Ten participants (3.5%) selected no environmental articles.
Supplementary Materials provide a detailed breakdown of these selection patterns by valence and personal relevance.
We also examined whether baseline sentiments, interest, urgency, and perceived knowledge were associated with message selection.
The full results are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
Table 1 summarizes the results of regression analyses predicting post-exposure environmental sentiments.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> summarizes the results of regression analyses predicting post-exposure environmental sentiments.

text.text: Hypothesis 1a predicted that greater exposure to positive environmental messages would be associated with higher hopeful environmental sentiment.
However, the coefficient for positive human-related message selections was positive but only marginally significant (β = 0.08, t(273) = 1.75, p = .081, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.18]).
The coefficient for positive animal-related message selections was not statistically significant either (β = -0.05, t(273) = -1.13, p = .262, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.04]).
Thus, Hypothesis 1a was not supported.

At the same time, participants who selected more negative humanrelated messages reported significantly lower post-exposure hopeful environmental sentiment (β = -0.15, t(273) = -3.06, p = .002, 95% CI [-0.24, -0.05]), whereas the coefficient for negative animal-related message selections was not statistically significant (β = 0.005, t(273) = 0.10, p = .921, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.10]).
Hypothesis 1b predicted that greater exposure to negative environmental messages would correspond to higher anxious environmental sentiment.

Consistent with the hypothesis, negative human-related message selections were a significant positive predictor of anxious environmental sentiment (β = 0.09, t(273) = 2.51, p = .013, 95% CI [0.02, 0.17]).
However, the coefficient for negative animal-related message selections was positive but only marginally significant (β = 0.07, t(273) = 1.90, p = .059, 95% CI [-0.003, 0.14]).
Thus, Hypothesis 1b received partial support.

Additionally, participants who selected more positive human-related messages also reported significantly lower anxious environmental sentiment (β = -0.08, t(273) = -2.09, p = .037, 95% CI [-0.15, -0.004]), while positive animal-related message selections were not significantly related to anxious environmental sentiment (β = 0.02, t(273) = 0.61, p = .545, 95% CI [-0.05, 0.09]).
the associations between participants' environmental message selections and their environmental sentiments.

Regression coefficient comparisons showed that, in the model predicting hopeful environmental sentiment, positive human-related message selections were significantly stronger predictors of higher hopeful sentiment than were positive animal-related message selections, F(1,273) = 3.91, p = .049.
For negative messages, human-related selections were more negatively associated with hopeful sentiment than animal-related selections, F(1, 273) = 4.12, p = .043.

In the model predicting anxious environmental sentiment, positive human-related selections were more negatively associated with anxious sentiment than positive animal-related selections, although the difference was marginally significant, F(1,273) = 3.50, p = .063.
Negative human-and animal-related message selections did not differ significantly in predicting higher anxious sentiment, F(1,273) = 0.17, p = .678.
Taken together, the results for self-selected exposure provided little support for Hypothesis 1a and partial support for Hypothesis 1b.

Positive environmental message selections were not significant predictors of hopeful sentiment, whereas participants who selected more negative human-related messages reported significantly higher anxious sentiment.
Evidence for Hypothesis 2 was mixed.

In the model predicting hopeful sentiment, human-related selections had a more positive association than animal-related selections for positive messages and a more negative association for negative messages.
For anxious sentiment, the human-animal difference was marginal for positive messages and nonsignificant for negative messages.
To address the research question of how post-exposure sentiments would predict participants' subsequent environmental information-seeking intentions, we conducted a parallel mediation analysis.

Specifically, hopeful and anxious post-exposure sentiments were included simultaneously as mediators linking message selection to information-seeking intentions, while controlling for their corresponding preexposure levels.
The structure and standardized path coefficients of the model are presented in Figure 3.
text.formatted: The structure and standardized path coefficients of the model are presented in Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>.

text.text: The overall pattern of paths between message selections and post-exposure sentiments was consistent with the preceding regression analyses.
Neither the estimated direct nor total effects of environmental message selections on informationseeking intentions were statistically significant.
However, both post-exposure hopeful and anxious environmental sentiments positively predicted information-seeking intentions.
Significant indirect effects were found only for negative human-related message selections.
Specifically, participants who selected more negative human-related messages reported higher anxious sentiment, which positively predicted information-seeking intentions.
The estimated indirect effect via anxious sentiment was therefore positive.
These participants also reported lower hopeful sentiment.
Because hopeful sentiment positively predicted information-seeking intentions, the estimated indirect effect via hopeful sentiment was negative.

Thus, the parallel mediation model showed two opposing indirect associations linking self-selected exposure to negative human-related messages with informationseeking intentions, although the total effect was not significant.

The results from Study 1 indicate that participants' post-exposure environmental sentiments were related to the environmental articles they actively chose to read, particularly in response to negative, highly personally relevant messages.
Specifically, participants who selected more negative human-related messages reported higher anxious sentiment and lower hopeful sentiment.
These contrasting patterns may help account for the nonsignificant overall association between selective exposure to these messages and information-seeking intentions.
The parallel mediation analysis estimated a positive indirect effect via anxious sentiment and a negative indirect effect via hopeful sentiment.

This pattern deserves further investigation, as it may help explain why communication strategies that emphasize a single emotional valence may yield limited behavioral effects: they may focus on strengthening one sentiment while overlooking changes in another sentiment that differentially affect information seeking.
In addition, the moderating role of personal relevance in the relationship between message exposure and sentiments received only partial support.
The failure to reach statistical significance may be due to the limited statistical power given the relatively small sample size of the exploratory study (Button et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The failure to reach statistical significance may be due to the limited statistical power given the relatively small sample size of the exploratory study <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Button et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, the pattern of coefficient differences suggested generally stronger relationships for human-related than for animal-related message selections, consistent with prior empirical findings (Arlt et al., 2018; Liu & Yang, 2023), and so we considered it worthwhile to test this in a confirmatory study with a larger sample size.
