text.text: Based on the findings in Study 1, a confirmatory study was designed to test (a) whether the association between people's selection of negative environmental messages and changes in hopeful and anxious environmental sentiments varied according to personal relevance (H1), and (b) whether people's selection of negative human-related messages was indirectly associated with information-seeking intentions through hopeful and anxious environmental sentiments (H2).
In doing so, we tested whether the two opposing indirect pathways observed in the exploratory study could be replicated.
The refined hypotheses are summarized as follows:

In the environmental domain, people's selection of negative messages was expected to be associated with changes in people's sentiments toward environmental issues, with the strength of these associations varying according to perceived personal relevance.
Specifically: • H1a.

People's selection of personally relevant negative messages is expected to be associated with a greater decrease in hopeful sentiment than their selection of less personally relevant negative messages.
• H1b.

People's selection of personally relevant negative messages is expected to be associated with a greater increase in anxious sentiment than their selection of less personally relevant negative messages.
People's selection of personally relevant negative messages is expected to be associated with information-seeking intentions through two opposing pathways, with sentiments serving as mediators.
Specifically: • H2a.
Selecting personally relevant negative messages was expected to be associated with a decrease in hopeful sentiment, which in turn was expected to predict lower information-seeking intentions.
• H2b.
Selecting personally relevant negative messages was expected to be associated with an increase in anxious sentiment, which in turn was expected to predict higher information-seeking intentions.
>Method
text.formatted: <head n="3.1." >Method</head>

text.text: To estimate the required sample size, a Monte Carlo power analysis was conducted based on the standardized path coefficients obtained from Study 1 (Muthén & Muthén, 2002) using the Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Indirect Effects web application (Schoemann et al., 2017).
text.formatted: To estimate the required sample size, a Monte Carlo power analysis was conducted based on the standardized path coefficients obtained from Study 1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Muthén & Muthén, 2002)</ref> using the Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Indirect Effects web application <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Schoemann et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The simulation included 1,000 replications and 20,000 Monte Carlo draws per replication, with a target power of 0.80 and a 95% confidence level.

Results indicated that the power to detect both indirect effects (via hopeful and anxious sentiments) reached target power at approximately N = 1,000, suggesting that a sample of around one thousand participants would be sufficient to reliably detect the mediation effects in this model.

The confirmatory study was preregistered on OSF (https://osf.io/gz3be/overview?view_only=89413f6597e54cd896304bbc0c9013be), including the updated hypotheses and the final analysis plan (Wagenmakers et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The confirmatory study was preregistered on OSF (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/gz3be/overview?view_only=89413f6597e54cd896304bbc0c9013be">https://osf.io/gz3be/overview?view_only=89413f6597e54cd896304bbc0c9013be</ref>), including the updated hypotheses and the final analysis plan <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Wagenmakers et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In this preregistration, Hypotheses 1 and 2 were pre-registered as confirmatory because Study 1 offered clear support for directional predictions.
Results for additional exploratory questions preregistered on OSF are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
A total of 1,034 participants were recruited from the United Kingdom via the Prolific platform.

After excluding twenty-five participants who failed the attention check or did not complete the task as instructed, the final sample consisted of 1,009 participants (438 women, 563 men, 4 non-binary/third gender, and 4 who preferred to self-describe or not to say).
Participants' ages ranged from 18 to 81 years (M = 42.55, SD = 13.51).
Most participants held at least a bachelor's degree (40.4% bachelor's, 20.7% graduate or professional).
Each participant received £2.70 as compensation for completing the study, which took approximately 18 minutes.
Ethical approval for this research was granted by the Ethical Review Board of the University of Amsterdam, and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation
The procedure largely mirrored that of the exploratory study.

Participants first completed baseline measures of sentiments (hope, optimism, anxiety, and worry), as well as control variables, namely curiosity, interest, urgency, and perceived knowledge regarding environmental issues.
Next, participants completed the selective exposure task.

Considering the available resources, the results from Study 1, the length of the survey, and our premise that inattentive reading reflects realistic online behavior, we did not include the memory test in Study 2.
After the selective exposure task, participants' sentiments toward environmental issues were measured again.
Unlike in the exploratory study, we also re-assessed curiosity, interest, and urgency for exploratory purposes, to examine whether these variables changed as a function of message exposure.
Subsequently, participants reported their intentions to seek further information about environmental topics.
Finally, they provided demographic information, including age, gender, and education level.
The materials used in the confirmatory study were identical to those in the exploratory study.
The measures were also consistent, except that the assessment of information-seeking intentions was simplified.
In the exploratory study, participants' intentions to seek further information were measured using five items adapted from Kahlor (2010).
text.formatted: In the exploratory study, participants' intentions to seek further information were measured using five items adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Kahlor (2010)</ref>.

text.text: The information-seeking scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency (α = .98), indicating that all five items assessed the same underlying construct.
To reduce redundancy, a single item was used to measure information-seeking intentions: "I intend to find more information about environmental issues soon."
This item was chosen for its conceptual clarity in reflecting a proactive and immediate intention.
Responses were recorded on a 7-point Likert-type scale (1 = Strongly Disagree,7 = Strongly Agree).

The primary, preregistered analyses in Study 2 followed the same count-based approach as Study 1, with the numbers of articles selected from the four environmental message categories entered simultaneously as predictors.

Although the hypotheses primarily focused on associations involving negative message exposure, particularly negative human-related messages, selection counts for all four message types were retained in the analyses.

This sought to allow for a more comprehensive examination of how selection of different message types was associated with both environmental sentiments and information-seeking intentions in a larger sample.
We conducted the same parallel mediation analysis for health-related articles in Study 2, with the results reported in the Supplementary Materials.
As a supplementary, non-preregistered robustness check, we re-estimated the regression and parallel mediation models among participants who selected at least one environmental article (n = 965).

These models represented each message category as a proportion of participants' total environmental selections, with positive animal-related exposure serving as the reference category, controlling for the total numbers of environmental and health articles selected.
This analysis examined the relative composition of message exposure.
The preregistered count-based models remained primary because they captured the absolute amount of category-specific exposure and included participants with no environmental selections.
Full details and results of proportion-based models are reported in the Supplementary Materials.
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="3.2." >Results</head>

text.text: On average, participants selected 7.59 (SD = 3.30) out of 16 available articles overall, including 3.57 (SD = 2.13) out of eight environmental messages, reflecting selective reading.
Results from Poisson mixed-effects models revealed a significant valence × personal relevance interaction, b = -0.23, SE = 0.07, z = -3.41, p < .001.
text.formatted: Results from Poisson mixed-effects models revealed a significant valence × personal relevance interaction, b = -0.23, SE = 0.07, z = -3.41, p < .001.

text.text: Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons showed that under negative valence, participants exhibited no reliable preference between human-related (M = 0.81, SD = 0.80) and animalrelated (M = 0.73, SD = 0.79) messages (z = -1.93, p = .107).
In contrast, under positive valence, participants selected significantly more animal-related (M = 1.08, SD = 0.78) than human-related (M = 0.95, SD = 0.79) messages (z = 2.97, p = .006).
Most participants chose environmental articles that varied in both valence and personal relevance.
Regarding valence, 702 participants (69.6%) chose both positive and negative articles, while 197 (19.5%) chose only positive articles and 66 (6.5%) chose only negative articles.

Selections also frequently spanned personal-relevance categories: 656 participants (65.0%) chose both human-and animal-related articles, compared with 126 (12.5%) who chose only human-related articles and 183 (18.1%) who chose only animal-related articles.
More than half of the sample (n = 563, 55.8%) selected articles from both valences and both personal-relevance categories.
Forty-four participants (4.4%) selected no environmental articles.
The full joint distribution is reported in Supplementary Materials.
We also examined the same baseline predictors of message selection as in Study 1, with full results reported in the Supplementary Materials.
Table 2 summarizes the results of the two regression models, with post-exposure hopeful and anxious environmental sentiments as the dependent variables, respectively.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> summarizes the results of the two regression models, with post-exposure hopeful and anxious environmental sentiments as the dependent variables, respectively.

text.text: As predicted in Hypothesis 1, selective exposure to negative human-related messages was associated with lower post-exposure hopeful environmental sentiment (β = -0.09, t(999) = -4.10, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.14, -0.05]) and higher anxious environmental sentiment (β = 0.08, t(999) = 4.28, p < .001, 95% CI [0.04, 0.12]).
text.formatted: As predicted in Hypothesis 1, selective exposure to negative human-related messages was associated with lower post-exposure hopeful environmental sentiment (β = -0.09, t(999) = -4.10, p < .001, 95% CI [-0.14, -0.05]) and higher anxious environmental sentiment (β = 0.08, t(999) = 4.28, p < .001, 95% CI [0.04, 0.12]).

text.text: Similarly, greater selection of negative animal-related messages also predicted lower hopeful environmental sentiment (β = -0.07, t(999) = -3.01, p = .003, 95% CI [-0.11, -0.02]) and higher anxious environmental sentiment (β = 0.05, t(999) = 2.68, p = .007, 95% CI [0.01, 0.08]).
This pattern of opposite associations across hopeful and anxious sentiment also extended to positive human-related messages.

Specifically, selection of positive human-related messages was associated with higher post-exposure hopeful environmental sentiment (β = 0.09, t(999) = 3.92, p < .001, 95% CI [0.05, 0.14]) and lower post-exposure anxious environmental sentiment (β = -0.06, t(999) = -2.92, p = .004, 95% CI [-0.09, -0.02]).
text.formatted: Specifically, selection of positive human-related messages was associated with higher post-exposure hopeful environmental sentiment (β = 0.09, t(999) = 3.92, p < .001, 95% CI [0.05, 0.14]) and lower post-exposure anxious environmental sentiment (β = -0.06, t(999) = -2.92, p = .004, 95% CI [-0.09, -0.02]).

text.text: However, exposure to positive animal-related messages did not significantly predict either hopeful post-exposure sentiment (β = 0.01, t(999) = 0.39, p = .695, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.05]) or anxious post-exposure sentiment (β = 0.00, t(999) = -0.12, p = .904, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.03]).
The moderating role of personal relevance proposed in Hypothesis 1 was not supported.

When predicting decreases in hopeful sentiment, the difference between negative human-related and negative animal-related message selections was not significant, F(1, 999) = 0.63, p = .426, providing no evidence for Hypothesis 1a.

Similarly, when predicting increases in anxious environmental sentiment, the difference between the two message types was also not significant, F(1, 999) = 1.27, p = .260, providing no evidence in support of Hypothesis 1b.
However, beyond the hypotheses, we observed a moderating role of personal relevance in the associations involving positive messages.

Comparisons of coefficients indicated that exposure to positive human-related messages was associated with higher post-exposure hopeful sentiment than exposure to positive animal-related messages, F(1, 999) = 6.09, p = .014.
The difference between the two message types in predicting anxious environmental sentiment did not reach significance, F(1, 999) = 3.79, p = .052.
The full parallel mediation model structure and standardized path coefficients are presented in information-seeking intentions were statistically significant.
Instead, several indirect pathways via environmental sentiments were observed.
As predicted (H2), negative human-related message selections showed two opposing indirect associations with information-seeking intentions through sentiments.
Greater selection of these messages was associated with higher anxious sentiments, which positively predicted information-seeking intentions, as well as lower hopeful sentiments.
Because hopeful sentiments also positively predicted information-seeking intentions, this reduction in hopeful sentiments resulted in a negative indirect effect.

In an exploratory and a confirmatory study, we used a selective exposure task to examine whether participants' selection of different types of environmental messages would be associated with their postexposure sentiments.
We also examined whether these post-exposure sentiments were, in turn, associated with intentions to seek further environmental information.
Across both studies, participants who selected more negative human-related messages consistently reported higher post-exposure anxious sentiments and lower post-exposure hopeful sentiments.
Both sentiments were, in turn, linked to higher information-seeking intentions, but their opposing shifts yielded indirect associations in opposite directions.
The total association between negative human-related message selection and information-seeking intentions was not significant.
With the substantially increased sample size in the confirmatory study, similar indirect-association patterns also emerged for positive human-related messages and negative animal-related messages.
These findings provide robust support for a dual-mediation model.
It shows that both hopeful and anxious feelings mediate the association between people's environmental message selection and their future information-seeking intentions, but in opposite ways.

Under selective exposure conditions, most participants selected a mix of positive and negative messages, as well as human-related and animal-related messages, rather than restricting themselves to a single category.
Their selections of three message types were significantly related to sentiment changes: negative human-related, positive human-related, and negative animal-related messages.
Taken together, these findings suggest a general pattern in which sentiment changes were more likely to occur among participants who selected more negative and personally relevant messages.

Although the observed associations were modest in magnitude (approximately .05 -.09 in absolute value), such effect sizes are not unexpected under conditions of naturalistic message exposure using real-world materials (Barabas & Jerit, 2010).
text.formatted: Although the observed associations were modest in magnitude (approximately .05 -.09 in absolute value), such effect sizes are not unexpected under conditions of naturalistic message exposure using real-world materials <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Barabas & Jerit, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: These effects can be understood in light of the negativity bias (Goldsmith & Dhar, 2013), especially given the salience of the ongoing environmental crisis.
text.formatted: These effects can be understood in light of the negativity bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Goldsmith & Dhar, 2013)</ref>, especially given the salience of the ongoing environmental crisis.

text.text: Negative messages heighten perceived risk and uncertainty (Tang et al., 2025), thereby amplifying worry and anxiety.
text.formatted: Negative messages heighten perceived risk and uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Tang et al., 2025)</ref>, thereby amplifying worry and anxiety.

text.text: Notably, this pattern appeared to be largely similar across the human and animal conditions, with no statistically significant difference between them in how message selection was associated with post-exposure sentiments.
This suggests that, when participants choose to engage with negatively framed messages, emotional charge may play a more dominant role than personal relevance in their affective responses.

In contrast, positive messages may rely more heavily on personal relevance to be emotionally engaging, as suggested by the stronger association between the selection of positive human-related messages, compared with positive animal-related messages, and post-exposure hopeful sentiment.

One possible explanation is that positive environmental messages may be less affectively compelling on their own, and therefore may need to be perceived as personally relevant in order to be appraised as emotionally meaningful and motivationally significant (Bayer et al., 2017; Lang, 2006; Schäfer et al., 2020).
text.formatted: One possible explanation is that positive environmental messages may be less affectively compelling on their own, and therefore may need to be perceived as personally relevant in order to be appraised as emotionally meaningful and motivationally significant <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bayer et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Lang, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Schäfer et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of a direct link between message selection on behavioral intentions highlights that any connection may lie in how the selected content relates to sentiment.
Below we elaborate on the possibility implied by these findings, namely that message selection and behavioral intentions may be linked primarily through affective pathways.

The present research aimed to examine the affective implications of selective exposure by investigating how people's active selection of environmental messages was related to changes in their reported sentiments.

Across both studies, participants who selected more messages from certain categories subsequently reported altered levels of hopeful and anxious sentiment, even after their baseline sentiments were taken into account.
These findings suggest that what people choose to read may be linked to their broader feelings about environmental issues.

These simultaneous, opposing shifts in hopeful and anxious sentiments are consistent with the Evaluative Space Model (Cacioppo & Berntson, 1994), which posits that positive and negative affective evaluations can exist independently, yet also exhibit an inverse association.
text.formatted: These simultaneous, opposing shifts in hopeful and anxious sentiments are consistent with the Evaluative Space Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cacioppo & Berntson, 1994)</ref>, which posits that positive and negative affective evaluations can exist independently, yet also exhibit an inverse association.

text.text: Specifically, participants who selected more negative messages generally reported higher post-exposure anxious sentiment and lower post-exposure hopeful sentiment.

This suggests that selecting environmental messages of a given valence may be linked to a shift in the balance between hopeful and anxious sentiments, rather than to a change only in the sentiment that matches the message valence.
This may be particularly relevant in environmental communication, where coverage frequently emphasizes crisis and loss.
Repeated exposure to such "doom and gloom" narratives may cultivate an affective orientation dominated by negative sentiment and hopelessness.
Crucially, these dual sentiment shifts also have implications for information seeking.
In our findings, higher levels of both hopeful and anxious sentiments predicted greater information-seeking intentions.
This means that both hope and anxiety may motivate people to seek further environmental information.
However, selecting more messages of a given valence was related to these sentiments in opposite directions.

In the case of negative messages, heightened anxious sentiment may form a positive pathway to information seeking, whereas reduced hopeful sentiment may create a negative pathway because hope also supports information seeking.
These opposing indirect pathways may therefore partially offset each other, attenuating the potential of selected messages to motivate further information seeking.

Taken together, these results question the effectiveness of exclusively threat-based or hope-based appeals, consistent with evidence that neither approach is uniformly effective (Brosch, 2021; Ettinger et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Taken together, these results question the effectiveness of exclusively threat-based or hope-based appeals, consistent with evidence that neither approach is uniformly effective <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brosch, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Ettinger et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Protection motivation theory further suggests that constructive responses to threats depend not only on perceived severity but also on whether protective actions are viewed as effective and feasible (Frantz et al., 2024; Maddux & Rogers, 1983).
text.formatted: Protection motivation theory further suggests that constructive responses to threats depend not only on perceived severity but also on whether protective actions are viewed as effective and feasible <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Frantz et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Maddux & Rogers, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Environmental messages may therefore be more effective when they integrate positive and negative elements in a complementary manner (Troy et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Environmental messages may therefore be more effective when they integrate positive and negative elements in a complementary manner <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Troy et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings highlight a possible affective reason for this balance.
Specifically, balanced messages may help avoid a situation in which one sentiment is strengthened while another sentiment that also supports information seeking is weakened.
For instance, crisis-focused messages may benefit from preserving hope and efficacy, while progress-focused messages may still need to convey that substantial challenges remain.
Our study has several limitations.

First, allowing participants to choose among environmental messages enhances ecological validity but limits the ability to draw causal conclusions, as selection counts may reflect both exposure and pre-existing selection tendencies.
Although the models adjust for baseline characteristics, it is possible that additional, unmeasured confounds affected the results.
The findings should therefore be interpreted as baseline-adjusted associations rather than causal effects.
Second, although we aimed to respect individuals' autonomy in information selection, the set of message materials provided to participants was necessarily limited.

This introduces the risk of the materials-as-fixed-effects problem: because only a small, non-random set of message stimuli was used, the observed effects may partly reflect properties of the specific articles rather than the intended framing manipulation (Clark, 1973).
text.formatted: This introduces the risk of the materials-as-fixed-effects problem: because only a small, non-random set of message stimuli was used, the observed effects may partly reflect properties of the specific articles rather than the intended framing manipulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Clark, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: To reduce the likelihood that the findings were driven by idiosyncratic features of any single message, each message condition included two articles.
Nevertheless, the generalizability of the findings should be interpreted with caution.
Third, we operationalized personal relevance by comparing information relating to human vs nonhuman animals.

This distinction was informed by pilot testing, which suggested that, within our stimulus set, human-related environmental messages were perceived as more personally relevant than animal-related ones.
However, this does not imply that human-focused environmental news is universally experienced as more personally relevant.
Individual differences, such as moral values, environmental identity, and emotional attachment to animals, may moderate perceived relevance.
Thus, the framing manipulation captures only one pathway to personal relevance and may not generalize across audiences or issue contexts.
Moreover, future work could examine the effects of self-directed information seeking when messages vary in terms of psychological distance as a proxy for personal relevance (Liberman et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Moreover, future work could examine the effects of self-directed information seeking when messages vary in terms of psychological distance as a proxy for personal relevance <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Liberman et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For example, it would be interesting to conceptually replicate the present design with messages reflecting different spatial distances (e.g., local neighborhood impacts vs. distant global regions) or varying social distances (e.g., threats to one's immediate family vs. abstract impacts on distant populations) (Hong & Jeon, 2025; Tang & Chooi, 2023).
text.formatted: For example, it would be interesting to conceptually replicate the present design with messages reflecting different spatial distances (e.g., local neighborhood impacts vs. distant global regions) or varying social distances (e.g., threats to one's immediate family vs. abstract impacts on distant populations) <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Hong & Jeon, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Tang & Chooi, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, our sentiment measures were intended to capture issue-specific sentiments towards (the future consequences of) environmental issues rather than immediate emotional reactions to messages.
However, because we administered them immediately before and after the selective exposure task, we cannot determine whether the observed changes persisted beyond the study.

Although the order of sentiment items was counterbalanced, measurement reactivity remains possible: completing the baseline questionnaire may have influenced subsequent message choices, and repeating the sentiment items may have anchored post-exposure ratings to earlier responses.
In addition, we measured information-seeking intentions rather than actual information-seeking behavior.

Future research could assess baseline sentiments in a separate session, include delayed follow-ups, and examine whether changes in reported sentiments accumulate over time and translate into observable information-seeking behavior.
Future research could examine the possibility of combining positive and negative content within a single environmental message.

Prior work suggests that integrating threat-based information with feasible solutions, as well as hope-based information with caution (Troy et al., 2024), may mitigate the oppressive impact of purely single-valenced framing while preserving motivational force.
text.formatted: Prior work suggests that integrating threat-based information with feasible solutions, as well as hope-based information with caution <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Troy et al., 2024)</ref>, may mitigate the oppressive impact of purely single-valenced framing while preserving motivational force.

text.text: Such mixed-valence messages may also evoke ambivalence (e.g., the threat is salient, but are the proposed solutions truly applicable?), which can stimulate further information seeking as individuals attempt to resolve this discomfort (Buttlar et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such mixed-valence messages may also evoke ambivalence (e.g., the threat is salient, but are the proposed solutions truly applicable?), which can stimulate further information seeking as individuals attempt to resolve this discomfort <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Buttlar et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies could also replicate and extend the present findings in more ecologically valid communication environments, such as those involving images and videos.
Compared to text-based messages, visual and audiovisual formats can convey richer contextual details, thereby fostering more immersive experiences.
Such formats may elicit stronger affective responses, with potentially longerlasting implications for engagement and behavior (Meijers et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Such formats may elicit stronger affective responses, with potentially longerlasting implications for engagement and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Meijers et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, although participants in the present study were free to choose which messages to engage with, the data does not reveal why people chose to engage (or not) with certain messages.

Understanding the motives behind choosing certain messages over others, such as uncertainty reduction, knowledge acquisition, perceived relevance, or affect regulation (O'Donoghue et al., 2023; Vivanco Carlevari et al., 2025), may help clarify what people believe to gain (or lose) when engaging with environmental information.
text.formatted: Understanding the motives behind choosing certain messages over others, such as uncertainty reduction, knowledge acquisition, perceived relevance, or affect regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(O'Donoghue et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Vivanco Carlevari et al., 2025)</ref>, may help clarify what people believe to gain (or lose) when engaging with environmental information.

text.text: This study shows that the affective outcomes associated with environmental message selection are not simply a matter of increasing anxiety or hope.

Rather, these patterns vary with message valence and personal relevance, with participants who selected more negative, human-related messages showing the clearest dual shifts in anxious and hopeful sentiments.
Because both sentiments were associated with greater information-seeking intentions, their opposing shifts may yield indirect pathways that partially offset each other at the behavioral level.
This may help explain why selecting more negative, humanrelated messages was linked to substantial affective changes without a significant overall association with information-seeking intentions.
More broadly, these findings highlight the importance of considering both positive and negative affective pathways when designing environmental communication strategies.
